findings.title: Offset subtraction shifts epoch-ms/ISO values one day earlier in UTC- timezones (initial render, min_date, max_date)
findings.suggested_fix: Branch on input form instead of applying a blanket offset: numeric epoch-ms (Python-serialized UTC-midnight) and ISO strings should be read with getUTC* (new Date(d.getUTCFullYear(), d.getUTCMonth(), d.getUTCDate())), while toDateString() strings (local midnight, written by _on_select) should be read with local getFullYear/getMonth/getDate. Better, normalize the model.value form in _on_select/serializer so there is one representation.
findings.why_it_matters: For users west of UTC (e.g. America/Los_Angeles), a DatePicker whose value arrives as epoch-ms (every Python datetime/date value, e.g. datetime(2019,9,20) -> 1568937600000) now renders Thu Sep 19 2019 instead of Fri Sep 20 2019 on first load, and min_date/max_date are shifted the same way. The old code was correct for this form in all timezones, so this trades the reported UTC+ bug for a new UTC- bug on the most common input path. The fix is only right for local-midnight strings like 'Mon Sep 16 2019' that _on_select writes; the model value can legitimately be either form.
evidence: Ran node with the old and new _unlocal_date on new Date(1568937600000): TZ=America/Los_Angeles old=Fri Sep 20 2019, new=Thu Sep 19 2019; same for '2019-09-20'. UTC, Europe/Paris, Asia/Kolkata, Pacific/Kiritimati give Fri Sep 20 for both.

Same node run on 'Mon Sep 16 2019': Europe/Paris, Kolkata, Kiritimati old=Sun Sep 15 (the reported bug), new=Mon Sep 16; Los_Angeles and UTC give Mon Sep 16 for both old and new, so the change only helps the string form.
Python side serializes dates via convert_datetime_type (bokeh/util/serialization.py:184, UTC-midnight epoch ms), so the initial value is always the ms form that regresses.

findings.title: max_date/min_date time-of-day in epoch-ms now crosses the day boundary in far-east zones
findings.suggested_fix: Same fix as above: read ms values with UTC getters rather than adding the local offset; do not shift an instant that is not local midnight.
findings.why_it_matters: A max_date given as datetime.utcnow() (as the new tests do) with a late-UTC time of day is moved forward a day in UTC+ zones: TZ=Asia/Kolkata with 2026-10-10T19:37Z yields Sun Oct 11 2026 instead of Sat Oct 10 2026, so the picker allows selecting a date one day beyond max_date. The old code returned Oct 10 in all tested zones.
evidence: node run: Asia/Kolkata and Pacific/Kiritimati msUtcNow old=Sat Oct 10 2026, new=Sun Oct 11 2026.

residual_risks: The model value has two forms (epoch-ms from Python, toDateString() local strings from _on_select) and the JS code has no normalization, so any single transform of the value is wrong for one of them.
Date.parse of toDateString() strings is implementation-defined (non-ISO), though supported in major browsers.
testing_gaps: No integration test asserts the initially rendered input text for a Python-supplied value (test_basic only checks the label), so the UTC- regression (Sep 19 instead of Sep 20) would not be caught.

test_js_on_change_executes asserts the displayed value 'Mon Sep 16 2019' after clicking; the assertion holds with the old code on a UTC host and only exercises the string path on a UTC+ host, so it is dependent on the host TZ and does not guard the ms path; no test pins TZ (e.g. via browser TZ env) across UTC-, UTC and UTC+.
max_date=datetime.utcnow() makes tests time-dependent and, combined with the offset shift, boundary-sensitive around midnight.
test_server_on_change_round_trip checks Python-side values via utcfromtimestamp, which never touches the displayed value, so it cannot detect the display bug.
